title: Is my baby ready for solids?
headings: When to start Signs your baby is ready If the first tries don't go well Babies born early Making first meals go smoothly
text: The signs to look for, and why about 6 months is the usual start. Most babies are ready for solids at about 6 months; not before 4 months. Look for the signs together: sitting with support, good head control and interest in food. Breast milk or formula is still the main food until 12 months. Most babies are ready for foods other than breast milk or formula at about 6 months. Starting before 4 months isn't recommended. Every baby is different, so look at your baby, not just the calendar. From 6 to 12 months, breast milk or formula is still the main source of nutrition. Solid foods gradually become a bigger part of the diet. Look for these signs together: Sits up alone or with support Can control their head and neck Opens their mouth when you offer food Swallows food rather than pushing it back out onto their chin Brings objects to their mouth Tries to grasp small objects, such as toys or food Moves food from the front to the back of the tongue to swallow If your baby pushes the food out and it dribbles down their chin, they may not be able to move it to the back of their mouth yet. That's normal: they've never had anything thicker than milk. Try thinning the food the first few times, then gradually thicken it. Or wait a week or two and try again. If your baby cries or turns away, don't make them eat. If your baby was born early, ask your pediatrician when to start. This app counts your baby's age from their due date (corrected age) where that applies. Milk first: breast milk or formula is still the main food. Some parents offer a milk feed 30 to 60 minutes before solids; at 6 to 9 months, solids add to milk rather than replace it. Pick a calm time: when your baby is rested and alert, like mid-morning, rather than late evening when they’re overtired. Limit distractions: turn off screens and make mealtime calm and focused.

title: Choosing and using a high chair
headings: Why it matters What to look for At every meal Hook-on chairs Good posture helps safe eating
text: What to look for when you buy one, and how to use it safely at every meal. Choose a sturdy chair made on or after June 19, 2019, with a crotch strap. Buckle the straps at every meal; the tray isn't a restraint. Sit your baby upright with feet supported, and never leave them alone in the chair. High chairs are linked to thousands of emergency room visits each year. Most injuries happen when a child climbs in or out, when the chair tips as a child pushes back or rocks, or when a part like the strap, tray or lock fails. A chair that can't be tipped over easily. A manufacture date on or after June 19, 2019. Chairs made since then must meet a federal standard for stability, restraints and warning labels. The date is on a label on the chair. If it folds, a lock that holds every time you set it up. Straps that include a crotch strap, not just a waist strap. For a secondhand chair, check that it hasn't been recalled at CPSC.gov. Use the safety straps every time, including the crotch strap, and adjust them to fit snugly. This stops your baby from slipping down. Don't rely on the tray to hold your baby in. It isn't a restraint. Never let your child stand in the high chair. Keep the chair away from counters and tables; a child can push off hard enough to tip it. Never leave your baby alone in the chair, and don't let older children climb or play on it. A chair that hooks onto a table isn't a good substitute for a freestanding one. If you use one when eating out or traveling, choose one that locks onto the table, make sure the table is heavy enough not to tip, and check that your child's feet can't push against a table support. When a baby has to work to hold their body steady, they have less control for chewing and swallowing. Head up, chin level with the floor, and back upright. The 90-90-90 rule: about a 90-degree bend at the hips, knees and ankles. A firm footrest: when feet dangle, the body is less stable, and so are the tongue and jaw. Upright, never reclined: don’t feed your baby in a reclined seat, car seat or stroller.

title: Purees or finger foods?
headings: Start smooth Then build up textures When finger foods fit in You don't have to choose Whichever way you go What is baby-led weaning? Choking and iron with BLW
text: How textures build up, and how spoon-feeding and finger foods fit together. Start with smooth purees, then move to thicker, lumpier and chopped textures. Spoon-feeding and soft finger foods work well together. Whichever way you go, sit your baby upright and stay with them the whole meal. At around 6 months, it's easiest for babies to eat very smooth mashed, pureed or strained foods. It can take time to adjust to new textures, and your baby may cough, gag or spit up while learning. As your baby's skills develop, move on to thicker and lumpier foods, then finely chopped or ground foods. Trying different textures helps your baby: Learn to accept and like a variety of foods Develop fine motor skills, like pinching and picking up food Develop chewing skills Once your baby can sit up and bring their hands or objects to their mouth, they can start feeding themselves finger foods. Choose foods that are soft, easy to swallow and cut into small pieces, for example: Small pieces of banana Scrambled eggs Well-cooked pasta Well-cooked, finely chopped chicken Well-cooked, cut-up potatoes or peas Small pieces of soft bread Spoon-feeding and finger foods work well together. Many babies eat purees from a spoon while they practice picking up soft pieces. By about 12 months, most babies can easily feed themselves with their fingers. Offer foods that dissolve easily or don't need chewing, cut small. Sit your baby upright, and stay with them the whole meal. Keep meals calm and unhurried. Baby-led weaning (BLW) skips spoon-fed purees: babies feed themselves soft, whole finger foods from the start. Your baby decides what goes into their mouth, how fast they eat and when they stop. Listening to appetite: putting your baby in charge supports their own hunger and fullness cues. Hands-on learning: holding foods of different shapes and textures builds grasping skills and comfort with new textures. Family meals: eating the same foods alongside you helps your baby learn by watching. Research, including the BLISS study, found that babies offered appropriately prepared finger foods did not choke more often than spoon-fed babies. Prepare foods to be soft and the right size, and stay with your baby while they eat. Iron needs planning: purees can easily include iron-fortified cereal, while self-fed meals need iron-rich foods like soft meats, beans or lentils offered on purpose.

title: What to offer first
headings: Any order works Put iron first One at a time Build variety Two types of iron
text: There's no set order, but iron-rich foods matter from the start. Foods can come in any order; there's no need to start with vegetables. Put iron first: meat, fish, eggs, beans, lentils, tofu or iron-fortified cereal. Offer one new single-ingredient food at a time, 3 to 5 days apart. For most babies, foods don't need to come in a certain order. There's no evidence that offering fruit first makes a baby dislike vegetables. From about 6 months, your baby needs iron and zinc from food. Include foods like: Pureed meat, poultry or fish Iron-fortified infant cereal Eggs Beans, lentils and tofu Offer one single-ingredient food at a time, and wait 3 to 5 days before the next new food. That makes it easier to spot a reaction. By 7 or 8 months, many babies are eating foods from every group: vegetables, fruits, proteins, dairy without added sugar, and whole grains. If you use infant cereal, rotate oat, barley and multigrain rather than only rice cereal, which can raise arsenic exposure. Full-term babies are born with iron stores that run low by about 6 months, while their fast-growing brain needs plenty of iron. Iron from animal foods (heme iron) is easier to absorb: meat such as beef and turkey, and fish. Iron from plant foods and eggs (non-heme iron) is absorbed less easily: beans, lentils, tofu, spinach, egg yolk and iron-fortified infant cereal. Your baby absorbs plant iron better with a vitamin C food, like lentils with tomatoes, or spinach with strawberries or a squeeze of lemon.

title: Introducing common allergens
headings: Early can help How to start Practical ways to prepare them Talk to your pediatrician first if Watch for reactions
text: Why offering egg, peanut and other allergens early can help, and how to do it. There's no benefit to delaying common allergens: offer them early, then regularly. Start with a small taste, one allergen at a time, early in the day. Call 911 for trouble breathing, lip or tongue swelling, repeated vomiting or unusual sleepiness. In the US, nine foods cause about 90% of food allergy reactions: milk (dairy), egg, peanut, tree nuts, wheat, soy, sesame, fish and shellfish. Families used to be told to wait until age 2 or 3. Newer research found no benefit to delaying allergens. The LEAP study found that offering peanut foods early, starting between 4 and 11 months, and then regularly, greatly lowered the chance of peanut allergy in babies at high risk. Start with a few low-allergy foods first, like infant cereal or pureed fruit. Then offer the common allergens one at a time: egg, peanut, dairy (like yogurt), wheat, soy, sesame, fish, shellfish and tree nuts. Start with a small taste. If there's no reaction, gradually offer more. Offer a new allergen early in the day, like at breakfast or lunch, so you can watch your baby for the rest of the day, and wait 3 to 5 days before the next one. Once a food is tolerated, keep it in the diet regularly. Always use a safe form: peanut and nut butters thinned, never chunks or whole nuts; egg fully cooked. Peanut: mix 1 teaspoon of smooth, unsalted peanut butter with 2 teaspoons of warm water, breast milk, formula or puree. Never give peanut butter straight off a spoon, and never whole peanuts. Egg: cook it well, as a fully set scramble or a hard-boiled egg, and mash it well. Tree nuts: stir finely ground nut flour (like almond flour) or a thinned smooth nut butter into warm oatmeal or fruit puree. Your baby has severe, persistent eczema Your baby has had an allergic reaction to a food, such as egg Food allergies run in your family (you can also talk to an allergist) Food allergies can be severe and life-threatening. After a new food, watch for signs like a rash, vomiting or diarrhea. If you see them, stop the food and call your pediatrician. Call 911 for trouble breathing, swelling of the lips or tongue, hives all over, repeated vomiting, or unusual sleepiness. If your baby has been prescribed epinephrine, give it right away. Most egg allergies are caused by proteins in the egg white, but the yolk can cause reactions too.

title: Choking vs. gagging: how to be prepared
headings: Calm, prepared and confident Gagging is normal Why babies gag Lower the risk Be ready before you need it Choking is an emergency
text: Gagging is a normal part of learning to eat. Choking is an emergency. Know the difference, lower the risk, and know what to do. Gagging is loud, red and normal: stay calm and let your baby clear it. Choking is often silent: act right away and call 911. Change high-risk foods, keep your baby upright, and take an infant CPR class. Few things make a parent’s heart skip faster than seeing their baby cough, sputter or turn a little red while eating. When you’re introducing solid foods, watching your baby handle new textures can feel nerve-wracking. Knowing the difference between gagging and choking, and knowing basic first aid, helps you stay calm at the table and let your baby explore food with confidence. Gagging is a healthy part of learning to eat. A baby’s gag reflex sits much further forward on the tongue than an adult’s, so when a piece of food is too big or unfamiliar, the reflex pushes it forward and out of the way. What it looks like: watery eyes, a red or pink face, coughing, gagging or retching sounds, and leaning forward a little. What to do: stay calm and keep your baby sitting upright. Don’t put your fingers in their mouth; that can push food further back. Reassure them calmly, for example, "You’re okay, you’re working it out," and let them clear it themselves. In babies, the gag reflex starts near the middle to front of the tongue and moves farther back as they grow. Gagging helps keep food from reaching the airway before it has been chewed enough. Gagging is loud and red; choking is silent. You can’t remove every risk, but safe food preparation and good mealtime habits lower the chance of choking a lot. Change high-risk foods: never serve whole grapes, cherry tomatoes or hot dogs, or large chunks of meat. Cut grapes and cherry tomatoes lengthwise into quarters, and cut hot dogs and other tube-shaped foods into thin strips, then small pieces. Skip hard and sticky foods: keep raw carrots, popcorn and whole nuts away from babies and toddlers. Never give nut butter by the spoonful; thin it with water, breast milk or yogurt, or spread it thinly. Always sit upright: no eating while lying down, crawling, walking, or riding in the car or stroller. Strap your baby into a high chair with their feet supported. Always watch: stay with your baby the whole time they eat, even for a few seconds. We strongly encourage every parent and caregiver to take an in-person infant CPR and first aid class. The American Red Cross and the American Heart Association offer them. Preparation turns fear into confidence, so your baby can explore food with freedom and joy. Choking happens when food or an object blocks the airway. A choking baby is often silent: they can’t cry, cough, breathe or make a sound; may be gasping or wheezing; may look panicked; or their skin, lips or face turn pale, blue or dusky. Act right away and call 911. This is a medical emergency. If your baby is under 1, these are the basic steps taught in infant first aid classes. They don’t replace hands-on training. Get help: if someone is with you, have them call 911 right away. If you’re alone, shout for help, and if you can, call 911 on speaker so you can keep your hands free. 5 back blows: lay your baby face down along your forearm, resting on your thigh, with their head lower than their chest. Support the head and jaw with your hand. With the heel of your other hand, give up to 5 firm blows between the shoulder blades. 5 chest thrusts: turn your baby face up along your forearm, still supporting the head and keeping it lower than the chest. Place 2 fingers in the center of the chest, just below the nipple line, and give up to 5 quick thrusts straight down, about 1 1/2 inches deep. Repeat: keep alternating 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts until the object comes out and your baby can cry, cough or breathe. Only remove an object you can see. Never sweep your finger blindly in your baby’s mouth. If your baby stops responding: start infant CPR. If no one has called 911 yet, call after about 2 minutes of CPR. Even if your baby seems fine afterward, call your pediatrician to get them checked.

title: Hungry or full?
headings: Signs of hunger Signs of fullness Let them decide Is my baby eating enough?
text: How babies tell you they want more, or they're done. Reaching, opening wide and leaning in usually mean hungry. Turning away, closing the mouth and pushing food away usually mean full. Your baby decides how much; steady growth and wet diapers are the best signs. From 6 months, your baby may be hungry if they: Reach for or point to food Open their mouth when offered a spoon or food Get excited when they see food Use hand motions or sounds to say they want more Lean toward the spoon or wave their arms with excitement Push food away Close their mouth when food is offered Turn their head away Use hand motions or sounds to say they're done Arch their back or get distracted Your baby doesn't need to finish the jar or the plate. Food works best when it isn't used as a reward or punishment. If you're worried about how much your baby eats, talk to your pediatrician. Portions at 6 to 12 months vary a lot from meal to meal and day to day, so trust your baby’s appetite. The best signs of enough nutrition are steady growth along their curve at checkups and regular wet diapers. If you’re worried, talk to your pediatrician.

title: Cups, water and juice
headings: A first cup Water Juice Cow's milk Open cups and straw cups Embrace the mess
text: When to offer a cup, how much water, and why juice can wait. Offer an open or straw cup from about 6 months, and expect spills. A little water is fine once solids start: about 4 to 8 oz a day. No juice before 12 months, and cow's milk as a drink waits until 12 months. From about 6 months, you can offer a cup with a spouted lid, a cup with a straw, or an open cup. Around 9 months, babies can start learning to drink from a cup without a lid; by 12 months they can drink from one as you hold it. Expect spills. Breast milk or formula gives your baby the fluids they need. Once solids start, a little water is fine: about 4 to 8 oz a day. Juice isn't recommended before 12 months. After that, if you offer it, give only 100% juice, no more than 4 oz a day, in a cup, not a bottle. Plain cow's milk as a drink waits until 12 months. Drinking from a cup takes different skills from a bottle or breast: rounding the lips, lifting the tongue and holding the jaw steady. Many speech-language pathologists and pediatric dentists suggest open cups and straw cups over hard-spout sippy cups, which keep the tongue low in the mouth. Open cups: small, shot-glass-sized silicone or rimmed cups teach your baby to lift the tip of the tongue, steady the jaw and close the lips to keep from spilling. Straw cups: straw drinking works the cheek muscles and keeps the tongue back in the mouth. Weighted straws let your baby drink at any angle, and straw cups are handy on the go. Spills are part of learning. Let your baby explore the cup without treating spills as mistakes. At this age the goal is learning the skill; breast milk or formula still meets your baby’s fluid needs.

title: Making and storing baby food
headings: Make it Store it
text: A few hours of prep can stock your freezer for weeks. Cook until soft, then puree or mash with no added salt or seasoning. Homemade food spoils faster: refrigerate leftovers and check before serving. Freeze purees in ice-cube trays and use within 3 months. Pick some fruits, vegetables and grains. Cook them until soft enough to mash easily with a fork; ripe banana and avocado can be mashed raw. Puree or mash, and thin with breast milk, formula or water. Cook with no added salt or seasoning. Remove fat, skin and bones from meat, poultry and fish before cooking. Remove seeds and hard pits from fruit. Homemade food isn't bacteria-free and spoils faster than food from a jar. Refrigerate what you don't use and check for signs of spoilage before serving. To freeze, spoon purees into ice-cube trays. Once frozen, move the cubes to labeled, dated bags and use them within 3 months. Later, mix cubes to make new combinations.

title: Foods to skip in the first year
headings: Not before 12 months Not for babies or toddlers Choking hazards Why salt is limited Why skip added sugar before age 2
text: Honey, added sugar and a few others that wait until later. No honey, juice, or cow's or plant milk as a drink before 12 months. Skip added sugar, salty foods, raw milk products and high-mercury fish. Change choking hazards like whole grapes and nuts before serving. Honey, in any form. It can cause infant botulism, a severe food poisoning. Cow's milk or plant milks as a drink. Juice. Added sugars, including sweetened yogurts, cookies and sweet drinks. Salty foods. Choose canned foods labeled low sodium or no salt added. Unpasteurized (raw) milk, cheese, yogurt or juice. Fish high in mercury, like shark, swordfish and king mackerel. Some foods are only safe once changed: whole grapes, nuts, chunks of nut butter, raw hard vegetables and more. See the choking guide in this tab. Babies’ kidneys are still maturing and can’t handle much sodium. Don’t add salt to your baby’s food. Food without salt doesn’t have to be bland: Warm spices: cinnamon, nutmeg and cardamom in oatmeal or yogurt. Savory herbs: garlic powder, cumin, coriander, oregano and basil on roasted vegetables and meats. Citrus: a squeeze of lemon or lime adds brightness without sodium. Taste habits: early exposure to very sweet foods can build a preference for sweet tastes over vegetables and beans. Tooth decay: sugar feeds the mouth bacteria that cause cavities. Crowding out nutrients: sugary foods fill little tummies without the nutrients needed for growth.

title: When your baby refuses food
headings: Refusal is normal It takes time Try this Phases are normal Who decides what
text: Refusing new foods is normal. Here's how to keep offering. Refusal is normal; it often means a food is unfamiliar, not disliked. It can take 8 to 10 tries, so offer again calmly, next to a food your baby likes. You decide what, when and where; your baby decides whether and how much. When your baby turns their head, pushes the plate away or keeps their mouth shut, it’s easy to feel worried or frustrated. Food refusal is usually a healthy sign of independence and of your baby listening to their appetite. Refusing a food often means it’s unfamiliar, not that they dislike it. Your baby may not like a food the first time. It can take 8 to 10 tries before a young child accepts a new food. Wait about a week, then offer the food again. Mix the new food with one your baby already likes. Eat the food yourself first; babies learn by watching. Give a simple choice between two foods. Freeze small portions so repeat tries don't waste food. Always put one familiar food your baby likes next to a new or previously refused food. Keep your tone calm and even: skip big cheers for a bite and disappointment when they don’t, so food doesn’t become about approval. Toddlers may suddenly refuse foods they used to love, or not want foods to touch. These phases often pass by about age 5. Talk to your pediatrician if you're worried about growth. A widely used approach (from the Ellyn Satter Institute) splits mealtime jobs: You decide what food is served, when and where. Your baby decides whether to eat and how much.

title: Picky phases: finding peace at the table
headings: Welcome to the picky phase Why it happens Share the job Ways to build a curious eater When to check in A long-term journey
text: Picky eating is a normal stage. Why it happens, and calm, practical ways to handle it without mealtime battles. Picky eating is a normal stage that often fades by about age 5. You choose what's served; your child chooses whether and how much to eat. Talk to your pediatrician if your child isn't growing or eats only a few foods. If your once-enthusiastic eater suddenly turns their nose up at broccoli, refuses whole food groups, or wants the same plain meal three days in a row, take a deep breath. You’ve reached the picky eating years. Picky eating is a normal part of development. It’s rarely about your parenting or your cooking, and the CDC notes it often fades by around age 5. Knowing why it happens, and how to respond without turning meals into a battle, can change everything. Starting somewhere between about 12 and 18 months, a few big things change: Growth slows down: babies grow very fast in their first year, roughly tripling their birth weight. In the toddler years growth slows, so appetite naturally dips and toddlers often need less food than you expect. Caution about new foods: many toddlers are wary of anything unfamiliar. This is called food neophobia, and it’s a normal stage, not a sign that something is wrong. A wish for control: toddlers have little say over their day, but they do control what goes in their mouth. Refusing food is often a normal way of testing independence. A helpful approach is the Division of Responsibility, from feeding expert Ellyn Satter. It splits mealtime jobs between you and your child: Your job: you decide what food is served, when it’s served and where it’s eaten. Include at least one “safe” food you know your child usually eats. Your child’s job: your child decides whether to eat, and how much. When you stop pushing, bribing or begging for “just one more bite,” the power struggle tends to fade, and meals get calmer for everyone. You can’t make a child love vegetables, but you can make the table a place where trying new foods feels safe. Eat together, family style: put the dishes on the table and let your child serve themselves, with help. Seeing you enjoy the same food is one of the most powerful things you can do. Skip the short-order cooking: don’t make a separate meal when they refuse. Just make sure one part of the meal is something they’re comfortable with, like rice, bread or fruit, and let them fill up on that if they choose. Keep foods separate: many picky eaters don’t like foods touching. Try serving casseroles, stews or sandwiches taken apart, with the meat, rice and vegetables in separate piles. Offer again, with no pressure: it can take 8 to 10 tries, or more, before a child is willing to eat a new food. Wait a few days and try again. Touching, smelling or licking a food counts as progress, so celebrate the small steps. Make it playful: arrange food into a funny face, or let your child choose between two vegetables. Talk to your pediatrician if your child is losing weight or not growing as expected, eats only a handful of foods, gags or vomits often at meals, or if mealtimes are causing you a lot of worry. Learning to eat takes years. By staying calm, setting clear routines and trusting your child’s hunger and fullness cues, you’re helping them build a healthy, positive relationship with food that lasts.

title: Moving to cow's milk
headings: Why wait until 12 months What to offer Not too much
text: What changes at 12 months, and how much is enough. Plain cow's milk as a drink waits until 12 months. From 12 months, offer plain whole milk or a fortified, unsweetened plant milk. Milk is a drink, not a meal: too much can crowd out other foods. Before 12 months, plain cow’s milk shouldn’t replace breast milk or formula. Hard on young kidneys: cow’s milk has more protein, sodium and potassium than babies’ kidneys can easily handle. Iron loss: the proteins in cow’s milk can cause tiny amounts of bleeding in a young baby’s gut, which can add to iron-deficiency anemia. Missing nutrients: cow’s milk doesn’t have enough iron, vitamin E or essential fatty acids for the first year. From 12 months, offer plain, pasteurized whole cow's milk, or a plant milk fortified with calcium and vitamin D, unflavored and unsweetened. Children 12 to 23 months need about 2 servings of dairy a day, which can include milk, full-fat yogurt and cheese. Milk is a drink, not a replacement for food. Too much can leave your child less hungry for other foods, and some experts say it can make it harder to absorb iron. Ask your pediatrician if you're unsure how much is right.

title: Physical healing and postpartum recovery
headings: Healing takes longer than 6 weeks Warning signs: get care right away Pelvic floor and core The hormonal rollercoaster Caring for a tear or stitches Caring for a C-section incision Food for recovery
text: Beyond the 6-week checkup: what's happening in your body, how to look after it, and when to get help. Healing takes months, not 6 weeks, so go easy on yourself. Heavy bleeding, fever, chest pain or thoughts of harming yourself or your baby need care right away. Low mood lasting over 2 weeks is worth a call: 1-833-TLC-MAMA, 988, or 911 in an emergency. Many moms feel they should be back to normal by the 6-week checkup. In reality, your body keeps healing for months after birth, and that's expected. Go easy on yourself. Your postpartum visit is a good time to bring up anything that still hurts, leaks or worries you. You don't have to wait for it: if something feels wrong, call your OB-GYN or midwife. Get medical care right away, or call 911, if you have any of these warning signs in the year after birth: Heavy bleeding: soaking through one or more pads in an hour, or passing clots bigger than an egg A fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher A headache that won't go away or gets worse, or changes in your vision Trouble breathing, chest pain, or a racing heartbeat Swelling, redness or pain in one leg or arm Severe belly pain that doesn't go away Thoughts of harming yourself or your baby Pregnancy and birth stretch the muscles that support your bladder, uterus and bowel (your pelvic floor), and the muscles down the middle of your belly. They usually get stronger again with time and gentle exercise. Pelvic floor exercises (Kegels) can usually start soon after birth. To do one, squeeze the muscles you use to hold in pee, hold for a moment, then relax. After an uncomplicated vaginal birth, many moms can start gentle activity like walking as soon as they feel able. After a C-section, full activity usually comes back around 4 to 6 weeks if there are no complications. Check with your provider before you start, and build up slowly. Some moms notice a gap or a ridge down the middle of the belly when they sit up. This is called diastasis recti and is common after pregnancy. Ask your provider or a pelvic floor physical therapist which exercises are right for you. See your provider if you feel pressure or heaviness in your pelvis or vagina, or feel something bulging at the vaginal opening. These can be signs of prolapse. Leaking pee, low back ache, or symptoms that get worse when you stand or lift are worth mentioning too. Ask for a referral to a pelvic floor physical therapist if you have any of these, or if you're not sure you're doing the exercises right. Your hormones shift quickly after birth. Many moms have night sweats in the first weeks, and skin changes from pregnancy often fade slowly over the following months. Hair shedding is common too. It usually peaks about 4 months after birth, and most moms have their normal hair growth back by their child's first birthday. In the first few days after birth, many moms have mood swings, sadness, anxiety, crying spells or trouble sleeping. This is often called the baby blues, and it usually passes within a few days. Postpartum depression is different: it's stronger and lasts longer than 2 weeks. About 1 in 8 new moms have symptoms in the year after birth. It's common, it's not your fault, and it can be treated. Talk to your provider if low mood, worry or tiredness lasts longer than 2 weeks or makes it hard to care for yourself or your baby. National Maternal Mental Health Hotline: call or text 1-833-TLC-MAMA (1-833-852-6262), free, 24/7. In a crisis, call or text 988. If you or your baby are in danger, call 911. A tear or an episiotomy can take many weeks to heal. Stitches usually dissolve on their own. Wait 6 weeks before using tampons or having sex, unless your provider tells you otherwise. Ice packs help with pain and swelling in the first 24 hours. After 24 hours, warm sitz baths can soothe the area. After you pee or poop, spray warm water over the area and pat it dry. Change pads every 2 to 4 hours. Drink plenty of water and eat high-fiber foods to keep stools soft. Ask about a stool softener if you need one. Ask your provider which pain relievers are safe for you, especially if you're breastfeeding. A C-section is major surgery, so give yourself time. Many moms need several weeks before they feel like themselves again. Once your incision has fully closed, ask your provider or a physical therapist whether scar massage is right for you. Don't lift anything heavier than your baby for the first 6 to 8 weeks. Care for the dressing the way your care team showed you. Showers are usually fine. Wait for your provider's OK before soaking in a bath or hot tub, or swimming. Call your provider if the incision gets red, warm, swollen or starts to drain, smells bad, or opens, or if your pain gets worse. Your body is healing and, if you're breastfeeding, making milk too. Regular meals with a mix of foods help you keep going. Breastfeeding moms need about 330 to 400 extra calories a day. Your needs for some nutrients, like iodine and choline, go up while you breastfeed. Eggs, dairy, meat and low-mercury fish are good sources. Ask your provider whether you should keep taking a prenatal vitamin or another supplement. If you lost a lot of blood at birth, ask whether you need extra iron. If cooking feels like too much, that's normal. Simple, one-handed meals count. Eggs, yogurt and cheese Beans, lentils and whole grains for fiber Lots of fruits and vegetables Lean meat and poultry Low-mercury fish like salmon, 2 to 3 servings a week Water within reach whenever you sit down

title: Infant sleep and feeding realities
headings: Feeding your baby, your way Breastfeeding (or chestfeeding) realities Weaning or switching to formula Formula feeding and combo feeding A pumping routine you can live with What newborn sleep really looks like Safe sleep, every sleep When to call
text: Survival strategies for the first months: feeding your way, what newborn sleep really looks like, and how to keep sleep safe. Newborns feed 8 to 12 times a day and wake often; that's normal. Breastfeeding pain is a reason to get help early, not to push through. Safe sleep every time: on the back, on a firm, flat, empty surface. Breast milk, formula or both: a fed, loved baby is the goal. Whatever you choose, and however it changes over time, you deserve support, not judgment. Newborns feed often. Most feed 8 to 12 times in 24 hours, as often as every 1 to 3 hours, including at night. That's tiring, and it's normal. A good latch is key. In a good latch, your baby usually takes in most of the darker skin around the nipple (the areola), not just the nipple. If it hurts or your baby is only on the nipple, slide a clean finger into the corner of their mouth to break the suction and try again. In the first days your breasts may feel very full, hard or sore (engorgement). It usually eases as your body adjusts. Feeding often, hand expressing or pumping a little to soften the breast before a feed, and cold packs between feeds can help. Pain is a sign to get help early, not to push through. A breastfeeding specialist (look for an IBCLC), your pediatrician or your OB-GYN can check the latch and look at things like tongue tie. Ask them before deciding on any treatment. Call your doctor if part of your breast is red, warm or painful and you have a fever or flu-like aches. These can be signs of mastitis, a breast infection. Get care right away for red streaks on the breast, pus or blood in your milk, both breasts affected, or symptoms that suddenly get much worse. Also call if you don't feel better within 24 hours, or if feeding stays painful. Moving to formula, combining, or stopping breastfeeding can bring up big feelings: relief, guilt, sadness, or all three at once. Those feelings are common, and none of them mean you've failed. Cutting back slowly is usually more comfortable for your body. A breastfeeding specialist can help you make a plan. If low mood, worry or guilt lasts longer than 2 weeks, talk to your provider, or call or text the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline at 1-833-TLC-MAMA (1-833-852-6262). All infant formula sold legally in the US is reviewed by the FDA to make sure it meets nutrition and safety requirements. No brand is best, and store brands are held to the same rules. Iron-fortified formula is recommended. Combo feeding, giving both breast milk and formula, is a real option that works for many families. Talk with your pediatrician about how to fit it together for your baby. Mix formula exactly as the label says. Never add extra water to stretch it. Don't make homemade formula, and don't use formula labeled for toddlers before 12 months. Check that cans aren't expired, dented, puffy or leaking. Ask your pediatrician before switching brands or types, especially for special formulas. There's no single right pumping schedule. Fit it around your baby's feeds, your work and your sleep, and ask a breastfeeding specialist to help you make it manageable. Storing milk safely takes the pressure off. These are the CDC's guidelines for freshly pumped milk: Room temperature (77°F or cooler): up to 4 hours Refrigerator (40°F or colder): up to 4 days Freezer (0°F or colder): best within 6 months, up to 12 months Thawed milk: use within 24 hours, and never refreeze it Leftovers from a feeding: use within 2 hours, then throw them away Freeze in small portions, about 2 to 4 oz, to waste less Newborns sleep about 16 to 17 hours a day, but often only 1 or 2 hours at a time. They wake often because they need to eat, day and night. Babies don't have regular sleep cycles until about 4 months. Longer stretches come gradually, and every baby gets there on their own timeline. Strict wake-window charts and programs promising a newborn will sleep through the night aren't part of official US guidance. Be wary of anything that makes you feel your baby is broken: frequent waking is what newborns are built to do. Things that can help: keep days bright and playful and nights calm, quiet and dim. From around 4 months, try putting your baby down drowsy but awake. These steps lower the risk of SIDS and other sleep-related deaths. They apply to naps and nighttime alike. Always place your baby on their back to sleep. Use a firm, flat surface that isn't inclined, like a crib or bassinet with a fitted sheet. Keep the sleep space empty: no pillows, blankets, bumpers or soft toys. Share a room, not a bed, for at least the first 6 months. Never sleep with your baby on a couch or armchair. It's far riskier than any other place. If your baby falls asleep in a car seat, swing or carrier, move them to a firm, flat sleep surface on their back as soon as you can. Swaddling doesn't lower the risk of SIDS. If you swaddle, stop as soon as your baby shows signs of trying to roll, often around 3 to 4 months. Don't use weighted sleep sacks, swaddles or blankets. Offering a pacifier at naps and bedtime can help. If you're breastfeeding, you can wait until feeding is going well. Keep your baby from getting too hot, keep their head uncovered, and keep smoke and nicotine away from them. Call your pediatrician if your baby seems hard to wake, isn't feeding well, has fewer wet diapers than usual, or you're worried. Trust your gut. In an emergency, call 911.

title: Practical life and mom hacks
headings: Clothes that fit the body you have now Easy, nourishing meals Grocery shortcuts Your first outings with a newborn Packing the diaper bag
text: Saving time and sanity when every minute counts: comfy clothes, easy meals, and your first outings with a newborn. Comfortable clothes for the body you have now are enough. Stock simple, one-handed meals and snacks, and follow basic food safety. Start outings small, and restock the diaper bag as soon as you get home. Your body keeps changing for months after birth, and that's normal. You don't need a new wardrobe, just a few comfortable pieces that make you feel like yourself again. If you had a C-section, soft high-waisted bottoms that sit above the incision, or low ones that sit well below it, are often more comfortable than waistbands that press on it. Ask your provider before using a belly band or support garment. Soft, stretchy leggings or joggers with a wide waistband Button-front or wrap tops, and nursing tops or bras if you're breastfeeding Breathable cotton underwear in a size up while you heal A long cardigan or overshirt that goes over everything Slip-on shoes, for when bending down feels like a lot One outfit you love, for days you want to feel put together When your hands are full, food that's ready in minutes makes a big difference. A little planning, or a friend's help, can stock your freezer before or after the baby arrives. Freeze soups, chilis, curries and casseroles in single portions, labeled with the name and date. Cool cooked food and put it in the fridge or freezer within 2 hours. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Frozen meals taste best within 3 to 4 months. Thaw frozen meals in the fridge, in cold water, or in the microwave, never on the counter. Reheat leftovers until they're steaming hot, to 165°F. Keep one-handed snacks within reach: cheese sticks, yogurt, fruit, nut butter on toast, trail mix, energy bites and hard-boiled eggs. Keep a water bottle wherever you usually feed the baby. Grocery delivery or curbside pickup can save hours a week. Keep a running list of staples in your notes app so reordering takes a minute. When friends ask how they can help, it's okay to say: "A meal or a grocery run would be amazing." Stock up on staples: frozen vegetables, canned beans, rice, pasta, oats, eggs and bread. Pre-cut fruit and vegetables cost a bit more but save time on hard days. Rotisserie chicken turns into sandwiches, salads, wraps and quesadillas. Leaving the house for the first time can feel huge. Start small: a short walk around the block, a quick coffee, or a visit to a friend. Each trip gets easier. Go at a time that's usually calm for your baby, often right after a feed. Know where you could sit to feed or change them, and give yourself permission to head home early. In the car, babies ride rear-facing in their car seat, with the harness snug and no bulky coat underneath. Lay a blanket over the buckled straps instead. Car seats are for travel, not for sleeping or feeding outside the car. Keep babies younger than 6 months out of direct sun. Use shade, light clothing that covers their arms and legs, and a wide-brimmed hat. Sunscreen is a last resort, on small areas like the face. Wash your hands, and ask others to wash theirs, before touching the baby. Restock the bag as soon as you get home, so it's always ready to grab. Diapers (one for every 2 hours you'll be out, plus 2 extra) and wipes A changing pad and a few bags for dirty diapers or clothes A spare outfit for the baby, and a spare top for you Burp cloths Feeding supplies: a nursing cover if you like one, or bottles and formula or pumped milk A pacifier, if your baby uses one A hat and a light blanket Hand sanitizer and tissues Water, a snack and a phone charger for you Your baby's insurance card and pediatrician's number

title: Say yes to meal prep: a lifesaver for new moms
headings: Meal prep as self-care Why it helps Skip the pressure: try micro-prep Foods worth making ahead Smart strategies One batch at a time
text: Small, stress-free ways to keep nourishing food ready, so feeding yourself is one less thing to think about. Meal prep is self-care: it keeps your energy steady while you heal. Try micro-prep: prep ingredients, cook once and eat twice. Choose one-handed foods, use shortcuts, and say yes to help. The early weeks and months with a new baby are a joyful, overwhelming blur. Between night feeds, diaper changes and learning your baby’s cues, a proper sit-down meal can feel like a luxury. Meal prep isn’t a strict diet chore. Think of it as self-care, and your secret weapon for getting through the day. Here’s why it helps, and how to make it work without the pressure. Steady energy for recovery: your body needs enough food, protein and fluids while you heal. Having food ready helps you avoid skipped meals and energy crashes. Fuel for breastfeeding: if you’re breastfeeding, the CDC says you need about 330 to 400 extra calories a day. Easy, ready-to-eat food helps you keep up with your appetite. One less decision: sleep loss makes every choice harder. Knowing what’s for lunch frees up mental energy. Less spending and less waste: a stocked fridge means fewer last-minute takeout orders and less produce going bad. Meal prep doesn’t have to mean six hours on a Sunday filling 20 identical containers. With a newborn, small steps work better. Prep ingredients, not full meals: roast a sheet pan of sweet potatoes and vegetables, cook a pot of quinoa, and shred a store-bought rotisserie chicken. Store them separately, then mix and match into bowls, wraps or salads in a couple of minutes. Cook once, eat twice: when you make soup, a casserole or chili, double it and freeze half in single portions. Use small windows: chop vegetables while the kettle boils, or roll a batch of energy bites while your baby naps. Choose foods that keep well, need little reheating and are full of nutrients. Overnight oats and energy bites: an easy, filling base. Make a few jars of overnight oats, or roll oat and peanut butter bites for a one-handed snack. Sheet-pan dinners: chicken, salmon, sweet potatoes and green beans can roast together on parchment for easy cleanup. Jar and grain salads: layer the dressing at the bottom, then sturdy ingredients like chickpeas, cucumber, quinoa and chicken, with greens on top. They keep crisp for up to 4 days. Soups and stews: broth soups, lentil chili and sweet potato coconut stew freeze well and are easy to reheat. Go one-handed: babies often want to be held at mealtimes. Pick foods you can eat with one hand or a single spoon or fork, like wraps, bites, bowls and smoothies. Use shortcuts: frozen steam-in-bag vegetables, microwave rice pouches, canned beans and prewashed greens all save time. Accept help: when someone asks “How can I help?”, ask for a homemade soup or a batch of muffins. Keep it food-safe: refrigerate cooked food and rotisserie chicken within 2 hours, eat leftovers within 3 to 4 days or freeze them, and reheat until steaming hot (165°F). Saying yes to meal prep isn’t about a picture-perfect fridge. It’s about feeding yourself well, so you have the energy to care for your baby. Take it one batch, one jar and one meal at a time.

title: A snack basket by your feeding chair
headings: Why you need one Why every feeding spot needs a basket What to put in it: the checklist 1. The drink station 2. Grab-and-go dry snacks 3. Shelf-stable comforts Setting it up for success Taking care of you, too
text: Why a basket of one-handed snacks and a big drink by your glider is a sanity saver, and exactly what to put in it. Keep one-handed snacks and a big drink right by your feeding chair. Pick low-mess foods that won't drop crumbs on your baby. Restock daily, and keep the basket out of little hands as your baby grows. If you’re in the thick of the newborn weeks, nursing or bottle-feeding around the clock, you may know this feeling well. One minute you’re happily feeding your sleepy baby, and the next a sudden wave of hunger and thirst hits you like a freight train. And, of course, your baby is now contact-napping soundly on your chest. You are physically and emotionally pinned. Enter the feeding chair snack basket: a simple, sanity-saving station that can make the postpartum days a little easier. When you’re spending hours a day in a rocking chair or glider, convenience is everything. A snack and drink station right next to your chair helps in a few big ways: No moving required: everything is within arm’s reach, so you don’t risk waking a hard-to-settle baby. Steady energy: making milk takes energy. The CDC says breastfeeding moms need about 330 to 400 extra calories a day, and regular snacks help keep you from crashing. Water within reach: breastfeeding can make you very thirsty. You don’t need to force extra fluids; keep a big drink nearby and sip whenever you feel thirsty. The key to a great basket is one-handed, low-mess eating: foods that won’t drop crumbs on your baby’s head or need a fork. A large insulated tumbler with a straw: keeps ice water cold for hours and lets you drink with one hand. Electrolyte drink packets, if you like them: an easy way to add flavor to water during long night feeds. Plain water is usually all you need. Coconut water: a refreshing change from plain water. Nut mixes or trail mix: healthy fats and protein to keep you full longer. Granola bars or energy bites: look for ones made with oats and flaxseed for fiber and staying power. Pretzels or whole-grain crackers: a quick, salty crunch. Dried fruit: mango slices, apricots or raisins for a quick, sweet lift. Applesauce pouches: the ultimate no-mess, one-handed treat (yes, the ones meant for kids work wonders for moms too). Dark chocolate squares: because postpartum life needs a little daily joy. Beef jerky or meat sticks: lots of protein to stave off midnight cravings. Choose the right container: a woven basket, a small caddy with compartments, or a rolling cart that sits right beside your glider. Restock every day: make it part of your morning routine (or ask your partner) so you’re never caught empty-handed at 3 a.m. Add non-food essentials: lip balm, a hair tie, hand cream and the TV remote. You’ll thank yourself later. Keep a small trash can next to the chair, so wrappers don’t pile up. Keep it safe: nuts, seeds and dried fruit are choking hazards for babies and toddlers, so keep the basket out of little hands as your baby gets older. Avoid hot drinks while you’re holding your baby. A snack basket is a small, loving act of self-care, and a reminder during the 3 a.m. feed: I’m taking care of my baby, and I’m taking care of me, too. What’s your go-to late-night snack? Add it to the basket.

title: Growth and milestones, without the anxiety
headings: Every baby has their own timeline Around 2 months Around 4 months Around 6 months 9 months, 1 year and beyond Tummy time and play Understanding your baby's cues When crying feels like too much When to call your pediatrician
text: What to expect in the first months, simple ways to play together, and how to read your baby's cues, at your baby's own pace. Milestones are ranges: many healthy babies get there a little earlier or later. Tummy time and everyday play help your baby build new skills. Call your pediatrician if your baby loses a skill or you're worried. Milestones are skills like smiling, rolling and babbling. The CDC lists the ones most babies (75% or more) can do by a certain age, which means lots of healthy babies get there a little earlier or later. Try not to compare your baby with friends' babies or social media. Watch your baby instead, enjoy what they can do now, and share any worries with your pediatrician. Your baby's checkups include developmental checks, with screening recommended at 9, 18 and 30 months. Things many babies do by now: Calms down when you talk to them or pick them up Looks at your face and smiles back at you Makes sounds other than crying, and reacts to loud sounds Follows you with their eyes Lifts their head during tummy time Things many babies do by now: Smiles on their own to get your attention, and chuckles Coos ("oooo", "aahh") and makes sounds back when you talk Turns their head toward your voice Holds their head steady when held, and brings hands to mouth Pushes up onto elbows or forearms during tummy time Things many babies do by now: Knows familiar people and laughs Takes turns making sounds with you, blows raspberries and squeals Reaches for toys and puts things in their mouth to explore Rolls from tummy to back Leans on their hands for support when sitting The CDC has free milestone checklists for 9 months, 1 year and older. They're a helpful way to see what's coming next, not a test your baby has to pass. Tummy time helps your baby build the muscles they need to lift their head, roll, sit and later crawl. You can start the day you bring your baby home. Babies learn through everyday moments with you, so play doesn't need special toys. Try tummy time 2 to 3 times a day for 3 to 5 minutes, for example after a diaper change or a nap. Build up to 15 to 30 minutes a day in total by about 7 weeks. Tummy time is only for when your baby is awake and you're watching. Sleep is always on the back. Get down at their level, or lay your baby on your chest so they can see your face. Talk, sing and narrate your day. Babies love your voice. Offer safe things to look at, touch and hear: a mirror, different textures, a rattle. Crying is how babies talk. They might be hungry, tired, uncomfortable, overstimulated, or just want to be held. Over time you'll start to recognize what your baby needs. Hungry babies often show early signs before crying, like opening their mouth when they see the breast or bottle, or bringing their hands to their mouth. Things that can help calm a fussy baby: holding them close, rocking or walking, gentle back rubs, white noise, a pacifier, or swaddling if your baby isn't trying to roll yet. You may come across "wonder weeks" or "leaps": the idea that fussy phases happen on a set schedule. That isn't part of official US guidance. Fussy stretches are common, but every baby has their own rhythm. It's okay to need a break. If nothing works and you feel overwhelmed, put your baby on their back in a safe crib with nothing else in it, step away for 10 to 15 minutes, and calm yourself. Call a friend or listen to music, then check on your baby. Never shake, throw or jerk a baby, however frustrated you feel. If you're struggling, call or text 1-833-TLC-MAMA (1-833-852-6262) or 988. Trust your instincts. Call if: Your baby is younger than 2 months and has a fever. Call right away. Your baby is fussy after feeding, spits up or vomits a lot, or isn't gaining weight. The crying sounds different, or your baby seems sick or hard to settle. Your baby loses a skill they used to have. You're worried about how your baby moves, plays, sees, hears or communicates. Don't wait: you can also contact your state's early intervention program. In an emergency, call 911.

title: Your guide to starting solids, week by week
headings: Starting solids Is your baby ready? Look for the signs Week 1: Smooth purees Week 2: Thicker purees and new flavors Week 3: Lumpy and mashed textures Week 4 and beyond: Soft pieces and finger foods Tips for success
text: How to tell your baby is ready, and how to move from smooth purees to finger foods at a gentle pace. Start with smooth purees, then gradually move to lumpier textures and soft pieces. Offer iron-rich foods early, and common allergens one at a time. Follow your baby's cues, and keep meals low-pressure. Starting solid foods is one of the most exciting milestones in your baby's first year. Moving from breast milk or formula to solid foods is a gradual journey of development, taste exploration and new textures. Breast milk or formula is still your baby's main source of nutrition until 12 months. In the beginning, solids are about practice and discovery, not filling your baby up. Most babies are ready for solids at about 6 months. Starting before 4 months isn't recommended. Watch your baby, not just the calendar, for these signs: Good head and neck control: they can hold their head steady and upright on their own. Sitting up with little support in a high chair or supported seat. The tongue-thrust reflex has faded: they keep food in their mouth instead of pushing it straight back out with their tongue. Active interest in food: watching you eat, reaching for your plate, or opening their mouth when food comes near. Growing well: many babies have about doubled their birth weight by this stage. Talk to your pediatrician about when to start, especially if your baby was born early. Texture: completely smooth and runny, like single-ingredient iron-fortified baby cereal, smooth avocado, or steamed and blended sweet potato. Goal: practice, not volume. Offer 1 to 2 small spoonfuls once a day, after a milk feed. Your baby is learning how to move food around their mouth and swallow it. Texture: slightly thicker purees that cling to the spoon, like yogurt or applesauce. You can start mixing flavors, such as pear with spinach. Goal: keep introducing new single-ingredient vegetables and fruits. This is also a good time to start offering common allergens, like peanut butter thinned with water, breast milk or formula, or well-cooked egg, one at a time, with a few days between each new one so you can watch for a reaction. If your baby has severe eczema or an egg allergy, talk to your pediatrician before offering peanut. Texture: lumpy purees or foods mashed with a fork, with small soft lumps, like mashed banana, fork-mashed avocado, or well-cooked oatmeal. Goal: encourage your baby to move their tongue and mash food against the roof of their mouth, instead of just swallowing. Texture: soft, finely chopped foods, small soft pieces, or easy-to-grab finger foods, like well-cooked carrot sticks, soft broccoli florets, or strips of tender chicken. Goal: move toward family meals. Let your baby feed themselves and explore different shapes, temperatures and textures. Every baby moves at their own pace. If your baby isn't ready for the next texture yet, stay where they're comfortable for a little longer and try again in a few days. Pediatric guidance suggests finger foods soft enough to squash easily between your fingers. Always stay with your baby and make sure they're sitting upright while they eat. Avoid hard, round or sticky foods that are choking risks, like whole grapes, nuts, popcorn and raw carrots. Follow your baby's cues. Turning away, leaning back or closing their mouth means "I'm full." Leaning forward or opening wide means "More, please!" Iron is key. From about 6 months, your baby needs more iron than breast milk alone provides. Offer iron-rich foods early, like pureed meats, iron-fortified cereals or mashed beans. Keep meals low-pressure. Mess is part of learning! Let your baby touch, smell and smear their food. No honey before 12 months, and no cow's milk as a drink before 12 months.

title: Freezer cube magic: 3 months of baby food in 3 hours
headings: Homemade food, without the burnout Why freezer cubes work The 3-hour plan Mix and match Freezer safety
text: Batch-cook single-ingredient purees, freeze them in cubes, and mix and match all month long. Freezer cubes give right-sized portions, less waste and more variety. Cook without salt, sugar or seasoning, and freeze within 2 hours. Use within 3 months, thaw in the fridge, and never refreeze. Lots of parents love the idea of homemade baby food. What gets in the way is exhaustion: steaming, peeling and pureeing a single serving every day wears you out fast. The freezer cube approach, popularized by food scientist Dr. Lisa Barrangou in The Amazing Make-Ahead Baby Food Book, treats each puree as a building block. One afternoon of cooking can save time and money and give your baby lots of variety. When babies start solids at around 6 months, they eat very little, often just a spoonful or two. A whole batch of sweet potato puree can mean a mountain of leftovers. Ice-cube trays, or baby food freezer trays with lids, solve that: Right-sized portions: a standard cube is about 1 oz, which matches a beginner eater's portion. Less waste: you only thaw what your baby needs for that meal. More variety: freeze single-ingredient cubes, like peas, carrots, chicken or apple, then mix and match them on the day. Set your kitchen up like an assembly line: Hour 1, prep: wash, peel and chop a mix of vegetables, fruits and proteins. Remove seeds, pits, skin, fat and bones. Group them on baking sheets or in steamer baskets so they cook at the same time. Hour 2, cook and puree: steam or roast until fork-tender, with no added salt, sugar or seasoning. Puree until smooth, thinning with a little cooking water, breast milk or formula. Cool the purees and get them into the freezer within 2 hours. Hour 3, freeze and pop: spoon the purees into trays, cover, and freeze. Once solid, usually overnight, pop out the cubes and store them in airtight freezer bags or containers labeled with the food and the date. Once your baby has tried each food on its own without a reaction, you can start combining cubes. New flavor combinations help your baby get used to lots of different tastes. Sweet and earthy: 1 cube sweet potato + 1 cube green peas Protein-packed: 1 cube chicken or lentils + 1 cube carrots + a little squash Breakfast bowl: 1 cube iron-fortified baby oatmeal + 1 cube baked apple or pear Use frozen homemade purees within 3 months. Thaw cubes in the refrigerator, never on the counter, and use them within 1 to 2 days. To warm, put the food in a bowl and heat gently, for example by setting the bowl in hot water or warming it on the stovetop. Warm meat and egg purees on the stovetop. If you use a microwave, move the food to a microwave-safe dish (not the plastic storage bag or container), stir well, let it stand for 30 seconds, and test the temperature before serving. Microwaves heat unevenly and can leave hot spots that burn your baby's mouth. Serve from a bowl, not straight from the storage container. Throw away food your baby's spoon has touched. Don't refreeze food that has been thawed.

title: One meal, two textures: how to feed yourself and your baby from the same pot
headings: One pot, two eaters Why “one meal, two textures” works Golden rules of family cooking with a baby
text: Cook one base meal, set aside your baby’s portion before seasoning, and change the texture so you both eat the same food. Cook one base meal, and scoop out your baby's portion before adding salt or spice. Change the texture to suit your baby: mashed, soft strips or small pieces. Introduce allergens on their own before mixing them into family meals. Feeding a baby who is moving on to solid foods is an exciting milestone, but making separate meals for adults and babies can quickly lead to kitchen burnout. The secret to simpler mealtimes, without giving up flavor for adults or safety for little ones, is “one meal, two textures.” Take a single base meal, remove your baby’s portion before you add high-sodium or spicy ingredients, and change its texture. That way you can feed yourself and your baby with the exact same ingredients. Saves time and energy: you only cook once, with less prep and fewer dishes. Encourages healthy eating: babies learn by watching. When they see you eating the same colorful, nutrient-dense foods, they are more likely to accept new flavors. Builds eating skills: changing textures gradually lets your baby develop chewing skills safely as they grow. Hold the salt and sugar: babies’ kidneys can’t handle much sodium, and the USDA Dietary Guidelines advise no added sugars before age 2. Cook the base meal without added salt or sugar; adults can season their own plates at the table. Watch common allergens: introduce top allergens (like peanut butter, eggs, dairy and sesame) one at a time first, before mixing them into family meals. Mind choking hazards: whole nuts, whole grapes, raw hard vegetables and large chunks of meat are choking risks. Make sure your baby’s portion is soft, mashable, or cut into age-appropriate strips.

title: Decoding cluster feeding
headings: The biology behind the fussy hours Survival strategies
text: Why some babies want to feed every 30 to 60 minutes for hours, especially in the evening, and how to get through it. Frequent evening feeds are usually a normal phase, often during growth spurts. Plenty of wet and dirty diapers and good growth are reassuring signs. Set up a feeding station, and share the soothing with a partner. Cluster feeding is when a baby wants to nurse or take a bottle every 30 to 60 minutes over several hours. It often happens in the late afternoon or evening. It can leave parents worried, but it’s usually a normal phase. Making milk: frequent nursing signals your body to make more milk to keep up with your growing baby. Growth spurts: cluster feeding often lines up with growth spurts, commonly around 3 weeks, 6 weeks, 3 months and 6 months. Day and night rhythms: evening breast milk contains more melatonin, which may help your baby develop day and night rhythms. Reframe it: cluster feeding is your baby communicating a need. It usually isn’t a sign that you don’t have enough milk, as long as your baby has plenty of wet and dirty diapers and is growing well. If you’re worried, talk to your pediatrician or a breastfeeding specialist. Set up a station: have water, high-protein snacks and something to read or watch ready before the usual evening cluster begins. Divide and conquer: a partner can carry, bathe or soothe the baby between feeds to give the feeding parent short breaks.

title: From messy to skilled: teaching your baby to use a spoon
headings: How spoon skills develop Three phases The value of sensory play
text: Spoon skills build slowly. A three-phase approach from pre-loaded spoons at 6 months to independent scooping after 12 months. Spoon skills grow in phases, so don't expect neat scooping early. Start with pre-loaded spoons, then try two spoons, then independent scooping. Messy hands-on play builds comfort with new textures. Using a spoon takes planning, a steady shoulder, wrist turning and depth perception. Expecting an 8-month-old to scoop and bring food to their mouth without spilling is asking too much. Spoon skills grow in phases. Phase 1 (6 to 8 months), pre-loaded spoons: load puree or mash onto a textured dipping spoon and hand it to your baby to bring to their own mouth. Phase 2 (9 to 11 months), the two-spoon strategy: your baby holds one spoon to explore while you use a second spoon to feed or show scooping. Phase 3 (12 months and up), independent scooping: your baby dips into the bowl and turns their wrist toward their mouth. Letting your baby touch, squish and smear food builds confidence and comfort with food. Exploring with their hands helps your baby learn where their mouth is, and getting used to textures on their skin makes new textures in the mouth less surprising.

title: Safe serving sizes and textures by age
headings: Changing textures as your baby grows The squish test
text: How to shape and soften foods for 6 to 8 months and 9 to 12 months, and the squish test to check softness. 6 to 8 months: soft, finger-length strips your baby can hold in a fist. 9 to 12 months: small soft pieces about the size of a chickpea. Many parents use the squish test: it squashes easily between your thumb and finger. Preparing food safely means adjusting how soft it is and its shape as your baby’s skills grow. 6 to 8 months, finger-length strips: long, thick shapes about 3 to 4 inches long that your baby can hold in a fist. Soft enough to squash easily between your thumb and finger. 9 to 12 months, small soft pieces: small pieces about the size of a chickpea as the pincer grasp develops. Soft and tender enough to mash with the gums. Before offering a solid food, press it firmly between your thumb and index finger. If it squashes easily without much force, it’s soft enough for your baby to mash with their gums.

title: Spotting and handling allergic reactions
headings: When reactions happen Mild symptoms Severe symptoms (anaphylaxis) Log it
text: What mild and severe allergic reactions look like, and when to call your pediatrician or 911. Reactions usually start within minutes to 2 hours of eating. Mild signs: stop the food and call your pediatrician. Severe signs like swelling or trouble breathing: call 911 right away. Allergic reactions usually start within minutes to 2 hours after eating. Knowing the difference between mild and severe symptoms helps you act quickly. Food allergies can be severe and life-threatening. If your baby has severe eczema, a known food allergy or a family history of allergies, talk to your pediatrician or an allergist before offering major allergens. A few hives or a red rash around the mouth, or mild stomach upset. Stop serving the food and call your pediatrician for advice, including whether to give any medicine. Hives all over; swelling of the lips, face or tongue; wheezing, coughing or trouble breathing or swallowing; repeated vomiting; pale or blue skin; or sudden sleepiness or floppiness. Call 911 right away. Use epinephrine if your baby has been prescribed it. Note what your baby ate, how much and what happened in the app’s food diary, and share it with your pediatrician.

title: Oral-motor milestones: helping your baby learn to chew
headings: How chewing develops Helping your baby practice
text: How chewing develops from munching to mature chewing, and why moving on from smooth purees matters. Chewing is learned in stages, from munching to mature chewing. Safe finger foods and teething toys help your baby practice, always supervised. Move on from smooth purees between about 7 and 9 months. Chewing is a learned skill that coordinates the tongue, cheeks and jaw. Babies move through stages: Up-and-down munching. Moving food to the side with the tongue, onto the gums. Mature, circular (rotary) chewing. Teething toys and safe finger foods: let your baby practice biting and moving their tongue side to side, always supervised. Move through textures: don’t stay on smooth purees too long. Moving on to mashed, lumpier textures and soft finger foods between about 7 and 9 months helps prevent trouble with textures later.

title: First teeth: how to brush your baby’s teeth
headings: Before the first tooth Once the first tooth comes in
text: Caring for gums before the first tooth, the right amount of fluoride toothpaste, and when to book the first dental visit. Before teeth, wipe the gums daily with a soft, damp cloth. Once teeth come in, brush twice a day with a rice-grain smear of fluoride toothpaste. No bottles in bed, and see a dentist by the first birthday. Wipe your baby’s gums every day with a soft, damp washcloth. Brush twice a day with an infant toothbrush and a smear of fluoride toothpaste about the size of a grain of rice. At age 3, move to a pea-sized amount. Don’t put your baby to bed with a bottle of milk or juice. Liquids that sit on the teeth can cause serious tooth decay. See a dentist by your child’s first birthday, or within 6 months of the first tooth.
